source_articles.excerpt: Scientists report the detection of one of the strongest "UFOs" astronomers have ever seen during observations of a supermassive black hole.

headline_options: Astronomers Detect One of the Most Powerful Ultra-Fast Outflows Ever Recorded Near a Distant Supermassive Black Hole
When 'UFO' Means Something Entirely Different: What Black Hole Wind Science Tells Us About Cosmic Evolution
The UFO Sighting That Has Astronomers Genuinely Stunned — And It Has Nothing to Do With Aliens
body_markdown:
## A UFO Sighting That Rewrites Cosmic Records

When a team of international astronomers announced they had recorded one of the most powerful **ultra-fast outflows (UFOs)** ever detected near a supermassive black hole, the terminology alone was enough to stop the science world in its tracks. In the world of astrophysics, **UFO** is a well-established acronym for a violent class of black hole wind — and the specimen captured by researchers studying quasar **WISSH13** may be the most extreme example ever recorded in a non-lensed cosmic target. The implications stretch far beyond a clever acronym, touching on fundamental questions about how galaxies form, grow, and ultimately stop making stars.

The findings, published as a preprint on arXiv.org by a team led by Giorgio Lanzuisi of INAF Bologna, represent the culmination of a multi-year observational campaign called **WISSHFUL** — a dedicated program built around the XMM-Newton space observatory and the NuSTAR X-ray telescope. Together, these instruments gave researchers an unprecedented window into the violent energetics of a quasar that existed roughly two billion years after the Big Bang.

## What Exactly Is a Black Hole UFO?

The term ultra-fast outflow describes the supercharged gas winds that billow outward from the accretion disk surrounding an active supermassive black hole. When those winds exceed ten percent of the speed of light, astrophysicists classify them as UFOs — a threshold that signals extraordinary energy output and significant consequences for the surrounding galaxy.

These outflows are detectable through a precise observational signature. Ionized iron embedded within the outflow gases absorbs X-ray radiation as it hurtles away from the black hole, leaving characteristic dips in the X-ray spectrum. Because the gas is moving at such extreme velocities, those dips appear **blueshifted** — pushed toward higher energy levels — allowing astronomers to calculate both the presence and the speed of the outflow with considerable accuracy. It is, in essence, reading the fingerprint of a cosmic storm.

## Cosmic Noon and the WISSHFUL Program

The era in which WISSH13 existed — approximately 2 billion years after the universe's birth — corresponds to what cosmologists call **"cosmic noon,"** a period stretching from roughly 1.6 to 3.5 billion years post-Big Bang. This was the universe's most prolific era of star formation, and it is also the period during which astronomers believe supermassive black holes were most actively shaping their host galaxies through feedback mechanisms like UFOs.

The prevailing theory holds that these powerful outflows heat galactic gas reservoirs, effectively suppressing further star formation — a process known as **quenching**. Understanding how this mechanism operated at cosmic noon is central to explaining why galaxies like our own Milky Way look the way they do today. Most previous UFO detections at this epoch relied on gravitationally lensed quasars, where a foreground galaxy acts as a natural magnifying glass. While useful, lensing introduces complications that can distort measurements. The WISSHFUL program was specifically engineered to bypass this limitation by targeting hyper-luminous quasars bright enough to study directly.

## A Two-Speed Storm Around a Two-Billion Solar Mass Giant

WISH13's central black hole is a colossus, weighing in at nearly **two billion solar masses** — and it shines far more intensely than models would predict for an object of its size. When Lanzuisi's team combined fresh XMM-Newton observations from autumn 2024 with archival NuSTAR data originally captured in 2017, two distinct absorption features emerged from the X-ray spectrum, each corresponding to a separate component of the same ultra-fast outflow.

The two components travel at strikingly different velocities. The faster of the pair moves at approximately **30 percent of the speed of light**, while the slower component clocks in at around **10 percent**. The slower wind appears to be a persistent, long-lived feature of the outflow, while the faster component shows signs of being a more transient phenomenon — potentially linked to shorter-duration energetic events closer to the black hole's innermost regions. Together, the two components are estimated to expel between **21 and 24 solar masses of material every year**, a figure that places this outflow among the most massive and energetic ever catalogued.

## A Layered Architecture That Matches Theory

Perhaps most scientifically significant is how cleanly these observations align with existing theoretical models of black hole wind structure. Researchers have long predicted that UFOs should exhibit a layered geometry: a fast-moving inner "spine" launched from the innermost edge of the accretion disk, encased within a slower outer "sheath" originating farther from the black hole. The WISSH13 data appears to confirm this architecture in striking detail.

Skeptics might reasonably ask whether two data epochs separated by several years can reliably support such conclusions. The team acknowledges the complexity, noting that the transient nature of the faster component adds interpretive nuance. However, the consistency of the slower component across observations, combined with the theoretical alignment, lends the findings considerable credibility. This is not a single anomalous data point — it is a coherent picture built from multiple independent observational threads.

## Why This Discovery Matters Beyond the Numbers

The record-setting nature of this detection is significant, but the deeper implication is arguably more important. Despite originating in a quasar from the early universe, the WISSH13 outflow appears to obey the same fundamental physical relationships seen in active galaxies far closer to Earth. That consistency across billions of years of cosmic history suggests the mechanisms driving **ultra-fast outflows** are not exotic relics of a younger universe — they are durable, universal processes baked into the physics of supermassive black holes themselves.

This has direct consequences for how cosmologists model galaxy evolution. If UFO feedback operated consistently from cosmic noon to the present day, then the same equations governing nearby active galactic nuclei may be reliably extrapolated backward in time, sharpening our models of how the universe's large-scale structure assembled itself.

## The Road Ahead: Athena and the Next Frontier

Lanzuisi's team is already looking toward ESA's forthcoming **Athena X-ray mission** as the instrument that could push these discoveries even further. With dramatically improved sensitivity over current observatories, Athena could potentially detect ultra-fast outflows in quasars at even greater redshifts — pushing the observational frontier deeper into the universe's earliest epochs and testing whether this cosmic consistency holds all the way back to the first billion years of existence. For a field that trades in some of the largest numbers in science, that is a genuinely exciting prospect.
